UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                         BEFORE THE
                           FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Southern Indiana Gas and Electric                          )
Company                                                    )
                                                           )

                                                           )
Midcontinent Independent System                            )

                               Comments of the Illinois Commerce Commission

           Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedures, 1 and the

Commission’s Notice of Filing issued January 6, 2026, setting January 26, 2026, as the comment

date in this proceeding, the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) hereby submits the following

comments regarding the complaint filed by Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company d/b/a

CenterPoint Energy Indiana South (CenterPoint) against the Midcontinent Independent System

Operator, Inc. (MISO) on January 5, 2026 (Complaint). On January 13, 2026, the ICC filed a

separate notice of intervention in the above-captioned docket and therefore is a party to this

docket.

I. Comments

           A. Background

           The ICC is tasked with the facilitation of adequate, reliable, efficient and safe utility

    services at the least possible cost to Illinois constituents served by electric public utility. 2 As

    such, the ICC has a strong interest in the outcome of this proceeding and its future impact on


1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213.
2
    220 ILCS 5/1-102.

                                                       1
     Illinois ratepayers. A substantial portion of Illinois is within the Midcontinent Independent

    System Operator, Inc. (MISO) footprint, and Illinois is also a member of the Organization of

    MISO States, Inc. (OMS).

          The F.B. Culley Generating Station Units 2 and 3 (Culley Units 2 and 3 or Culley) are

    coal-fired electric generation facilities located in Indiana within MISO’s Region. Culley is

    owned and operated by CenterPoint. Culley Unit 2 (103.7 MW) and Unit 3 (265.2 MW) began

    commercial operations in 1966 and 1973, respectively. Culley Unit 2 has been subject to long-

    term retirement planning and was scheduled for retirement in December 2025 consistent with

    CenterPoint’s state-reviewed integrated resource plans (IRPs). Currently Unit 2 is on

    maintenance outage. 3

          Pursuant to section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act (FPA), on December 23, 2025, the

United States Secretary of Energy (Secretary or DOE) issued Department of Energy Order No.

202-25-13 (Culley Order). 4 The Secretary found that there is an emergency situation related to

resource adequacy existing in MISO’s territory and, therefore, the Secretary directed Culley Unit

2 to remain operational for a period of 90 days. 5 Specifically, in the Culley Order, the DOE

directed MISO and CenterPoint to inter alia “take all measures necessary to ensure that Culley

Unit 2 is available to operate” until March 23, 2026. 6 The DOE further directed CenterPoint to

“file with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Tariff revisions or waivers to effectuate

this Order, as needed. Rate recovery is available pursuant to 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c).” 7 Thereafter,

number-202-25-13-culley.

 CenterPoint filed its Complaint in the above-captioned docket seeking, inter alia, cost recovery

and allocation.

        The Commission should not approve CenterPoint’s request for rate recovery at this time.

The DOE’s unprecedented use of section 202(c) emergency orders 8 to continue the operation of

many coal-fired generation plants slated for immediate retirement will result in significant, but

currently unknown costs with unknown benefits. The Commission should direct CenterPoint to

provide further cost and benefit information, direct that the parties provide for a stakeholder

process to vet the appropriate mechanism for cost recovery under section 202(c) of the FPA 9 and,

at the appropriate time, set the matter for hearing to ensure a robust record that has the benefit of

the results of a stakeholder process on this issue. Further, the Complaint would impose cost

increases on ratepayers without any demonstrable commensurate benefits.

        B. Given the Volume of DOE 202(c) Orders, and the Potential Harmful Impacts on
        Ratepayers across the MISO Region, a Robust Stakeholder Process Is Needed

        In the Culley Order, the DOE asserts its decision to continue operating the Culley plant is

supported by reports by MISO, Organization of MISO States (OMS), and the North American

Electric Reliability Council (NERC), including MISO’s shift to a seasonal capacity auction, the

Attributes Roadmap, the Reliability Imperative, the most 2025-2026 Planning Resource Auction

(PRA) results, and the OMS-MISO survey. 10 Based on its flawed interpretation of those reports,

the DOE argues that emergency conditions exist and persist in the MISO footprint which

section-202c-craig-order-no-202-25-14.

                                                       3
 necessitate the Culley Unit 2 continued operation. 11 The reports relied on by the DOE do not

support an emergency order and continued operation of scheduled-to-retire coal generation plants

will result in harm to consumers from unnecessary cost increases and related rate increases.

        In the ICC’s comments to FERC in response to a similar emergency order issued by the

DOE related to the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Docket No. EL25-90-000 (Campbell Docket), the

ICC requested the Commission return the emergency order rate schedule to MISO. 12 In

addition, the ICC asserted that rate schedules should be subject to a robust and transparent

process where stakeholders can offer insight and provide necessary information. 13 A transparent

stakeholder process on rates ensures that benefit metrics are vetted and cost causers identified.

Ultimately, a stakeholder process that considers state preferences is fully in line with other

Commission actions. 14

        In the Commission’s order on rehearing in the Campbell Docket, however, the

Commission held that a MISO stakeholder process was not necessary to set rates. 15 The

Commission found that states and stakeholders were given an opportunity to provide input into

the emergency order process. 16 Specifically, the Commission found that the Campbell Docket,

“provided any interested stakeholder notice of Consumers’ proposal and an opportunity to

comment.” 17 In the Campbell decision, the Commission stressed that no stakeholder process was

needed since there was already sufficient information in the record to make a just and reasonable

 decision. 18 With these assertions in hand, the Commission denied the Campbell requests for

rehearing and accepted Consumers Energy cost allocation proposal. 19

         Since the Commission’s decision in the Campbell Docket, however, the DOE has now

issued two more emergency 202(c) orders in the MISO footprint alone, the Culley Order and

another for the R.M. Schahfer Generating Units 17 and 18 (Schahfer Order). 20 DOE’s emergency

orders are becoming routine. Further, there is nothing in the Culley Order or the Schahfer Order

that suggests this will be the last order or that these orders will be temporary. 21 In fact, the DOE

has extended its prior orders to keep retiring coal plants operating. 22 Given this, it seems likely

that current 202(c) orders will be extended and that more orders are likely to be issued,

potentially for years. The likely frequency and length of these orders, much longer than initial

90-day period, is crucial in considering how to handle cost allocation for generating units that are

unexpectedly and unnecessarily being retained on the system.

         The likelihood of more DOE emergency orders being issued is further supported by the

DOE’s definition of an alleged emergency. 23 The ICC agrees that DOE and the Commission have

the authority to both maintain energy reliability during emergency conditions as well as the

authority to set rates in those cases. However, it is not clear the current circumstances are

   FPA section 202(c)(1) provides that whenever the Secretary of Energy determines “that an emergency exists by
reason of a sudden increase in the demand for electric energy, or a shortage of electric energy or of facilities for the
generation or transmission of electric energy,” then the Secretary has the authority “to require by order . . . such
generation, delivery, interchange, or transmission of electric energy as in its judgment will best meet the emergency
and serve the public interest.” 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c). Although the text of FPA section 202(c) grants this authority to
“the Commission,” section 301(b) of the Department of Energy Organization Act transferred this authority to the
Secretary of Energy. See 42 U.S.C. § 7151(b).

 emergency situations. 24 Regardless of MISO’s actual capacity situation, the DOE uses its

Campbell Order rehearing denial to lay out broad definition of what an emergency is. The DOE

notes that “Congress accorded the Secretary [of Energy] discretion to determine the existence of

an emergency.” 25 There is no indication of an actual emergency and not indication that that the

orders issued in 2025 resolve the emergency situation if it existed. In fact, it is likely that the

DOE will continue to issue more. Thus, the situation is different than when cost allocation for

Campbell was decided this summer. The DOE’s understanding of emergency powers increases

the likelihood of more emergency orders being issued in the coming months. Thus, the

Commission should consider a more fulsome process to review cost allocation for these alleged

emergencies. Further, the problems the DOE Order alleges it will correct will likely occur, if

ever, after the 90 days of the order’s duration. 26 Likely extensions of the Culley Order means

that fast action is unnecessary and a more thoughtful examination is warranted.

        Because several persistent conditions remain, it is reasonable for the Commission not to

merely grant CenterPoint a rate schedule that the Commission deems best, but instead, the

Commission should return this issue to MISO and its stakeholder process so that rates can be

developed in an informed, open manner. Again, in this proceeding, the ICC is not requesting the

Commission here challenge or undo a DOE’s emergency order to the extent that the commission

 may determine that one actually exists. Rather, the ICC is asking the Commission to

acknowledge how this is becoming common practice and recognize that a flurry of Commission

decisions on emergency order cost allocation without the thorough vetting of a stakeholder

process could lead to unjust and unreasonable rates.

     C. Given the Questionable Economic and Emergency Claims of this Complaint, a More
        Thorough Stakeholder Process is Necessary

        The CenterPoint complaint rests on CenterPoint’s need to be reimbursed as a result of the

DOE’s emergency orders in absence of an existing MISO tariff for this circumstance. 27 The ICC

agrees that CenterPoint should be reimbursed for continuing to operate Culley Unit 2. However,

rather than relying on a quick Commission decision in response to CenterPoint’s complaint, the

Culley Order and related CenterPoint Complaint requires a more thorough stakeholder process at

MISO to determine the appropriate rate schedule. Spreading costs among MISO’s Zones 1-7

based on load ratio share, as was done in the Campbell decision, without a thorough

investigation is not reasonable – particularly given the questionable nature of this emergency and

potentially unnecessary expenditures that may result directly from this proceeding. 28

        A more robust stakeholder process is necessary, in part, because the capacity provided by

Culley Unit 2 is currently not needed in the MISO footprint. MISO has indicated that the

footprint currently has sufficient capacity for the current year. While MISO acknowledged an

elevated risk due to the potential for extreme weather events and the continued decline in

accredited capacity, MISO also anticipates adequate resources to serve summer demand during

the 2025/2026 year, the period to which the DOE Order applies. 29 Peak demand in MISO could

28

29

                                                      7
 reach nearly 123 gigawatts (GWs), with about 138 GWs of regularly available generation

expected across the MISO footprint, 15 GWs more than the estimated peak. 30 Further, MISO has

emergency operating measures, such as load modifying resources, already in place and ready to

be activated. 31 These factual circumstances demonstrated by MISO, seriously undermine the

DOE’s conclusion that an emergency situation exists or that an emergency order is needed. The

DOE order interrupts and distorts those mechanisms, resulting in excessive costs and slowing

down needed changes to the fleet. The DOE order puts MISO in a catch-22: by planning for its

future, MISO and its states become subject to unneeded, unrequested interventions by DOE that

disrupt state-endorsed practices, including plans by MISO, which FERC approved, 32 which

would address the very concerns the DOE is seeking to resolve.

        In addition to being unnecessary because there is no capacity emergency in MISO, the

DOE order is uneconomic. Culley Unit 2 has been scheduled to close since CenterPoint’s

2022/2023 IRP. 33 Culley Unit 2 is not being closed due to state policy but rather because it is

uneconomic. 34 Culley Unit 2 is unable to earn back its operating costs through the PRA or

contracts. 35 The plant is aging and keeping the plant operating could incur significant costs

which may be imprudent. Operating an unneeded, uneconomic plant will lead to significant

 consumer costs with negligible benefits. With the Culley Unit 2’s recent poorly performing

economic history in mind, a MISO stakeholder process to determine cost allocation is critical. A

stakeholder process will enable a careful accounting of the costs and benefits of operating Culley

Unit 2, including identifying who benefits from delaying this generator’s retirement to properly

assign costs. 36 Identifying beneficiaries is an important part of maintaining a fair, effective

market construct and it is particularly crucial when so many questions about the necessity of the

Culley plant’s ongoing operation remain.

        Finally, the DOE order is an overreach of federal authority. Resource adequacy and fuel

choice is state jurisdictional under section 201 of the Federal Power Act. 37 There is nothing to

suggest that Indiana was not taking the capacity concerns raised by retiring Culley Unit 2

seriously. Indiana and its utilities have a robust IRP process to plan around load changes,

retirements, and new resource additions. 38 The DOE’s broad definition of risk undermines the

very systems states and regional transmission organizations (RTOs) use to ensure reliability.

Market constructs, IRPs, reliability studies, and other industry practices are less useful when

unsubstantiated emergency orders interrupt them and distort market signals. Resource planning

requires time to gather data and to make decisions about future resources, and market constructs

also need an opportunity to respond to changing conditions. The Culley Order is now one of

many DOE 202(c) orders, reinforcing the recognition that the federal government is not

addressing a one off emergency but moving into state jurisdictional resource adequacy planning.

Congress has required that resource adequacy and fuel source decisions remain under state




36
   The ICC maintains that costs should align with benefits. Here, there has been no showing of quantifiable benefits
to Illinois ratepayers. See ICC June Comments.
37
    16 U.S.C. § 824(a),(b)(1).
38

division/electricity-industry/integrated-resource-plans/.

                                                         9
 jurisdiction. This works in part because states have the power to set rates or procure needed

power through market mechanisms. 39 Thus, a stakeholder process discussing how these

associated costs should be allocated is needed, and the Commission should provide sufficient

time to do so.

           The argument that Culley Unit 2 is unneeded, uneconomic, and beyond federal authority

seems, at first glance, beyond the scope of CenterPoint’s complaint, which is only asking for a

rate schedule. However, the reasoning for the predicate emergency demonstrates exactly why a

stakeholder process, rather than a more focused hearing process or Commission decision, is

needed. The FERC order on the Campbell plant rehearing asserts that the DOE’s instant

proceeding was a sufficient stakeholder process. 40 The ICC believes this is not sufficient given

the scale and scope of this order, the others happening in MISO and across the United States, and

ones likely to follow. MISO’s stakeholder process allows for more data transparency and

exploration of alternative ideas which ultimately lead to better solutions. In addition, the rapid

timelines the DOE and FERC have provided stakeholders make it especially difficult for states,

which represent ratepayers, to provide thorough and detailed comments.

       Given these emergency orders risk subjecting ratepayers to unnecessary costs on what is a

state jurisdictional issue as well as the Commission’s commitment to just and reasonable rates, it

is imperative that this issue be vetted through a transparent MISO stakeholder process. As

demonstrated by the above discussion, there are reasonable questions about resource adequacy in

MISO and how MISO plans to address them. A proper stakeholder process allows for a more

complete vetting of the relevant data. In addition, a robust stakeholder process will ensure that

cost allocation aligns with benefits because there will be a more detailed vetting of costs and


39
     16 U.S.C. § 824(a),(b)(1).
40
     193 FERC ¶ 61, 228 P 25.

                                                  10
 benefits of running these plants. While the Commission has raised concerns whether an RTO

stakeholder process is nimble enough to make a decision on emergency order rates, the ICC

believes that even an expedited MISO process is preferable to the Commission issuing a rate

schedule without fulsome stakeholder input. The ICC urges the Commission to order such a

process be undertaken, or, in the alternative, set the matter for a hearing on the record.

II. Conclusion

       WHEREFORE, for all the reasons explained above, the ICC respectfully requests that the

Commission consider these comments. The Commission should direct CenterPoint and MISO to

provide further cost and benefit information, direct that the parties provide for a stakeholder

process to vet the appropriate mechanism for cost recovery under section 202(c) in the event of

an emergency in a MISO stakeholder proceeding, or, in the alternative, set the matter for hearing

to ensure a robust record. The ICC further requests all other appropriate relief.

                                                      Respectfully submitted,
